$comment: Acceptance criteria for issue 171. completion.py's own resolution text says 'split the uncovered part into its own authority with its own bar', and nothing implements the state after you follow it: the parent keeps reading the prose and keeps answering CONTINUE forever. Six bars on disk carry a covers block. Issue 117 is the historical precedent -- its covers says in as many words 'split out to issue 131 by hand AFTER this bar had already read STOP_COMPLETE' -- and 143, 154, 155 and 156 are live. THE REFUSAL MUST SURVIVE. A bar may not become complete by deleting `covers`; it must POINT at where the uncovered work went, and the pointer is checked by evaluating those authorities rather than by trusting the text. An unresolvable or outstanding child leaves the parent CONTINUE. WHAT THIS DOES NOT DO, said plainly because the issue could be read as promising it: it does not close three issues today. Issue 155 points at 156, which still carries branch-dependence, so 155 correctly stays CONTINUE -- and unblocking it requires filing branch-dependence as its own authority. The mechanism FORCES THE CHAIN TO BE EXPLICIT rather than closing anything. TWO HAZARDS ARE CRITERIA, NOT COMMENTS. A cycle must be reported as a typed refusal rather than recursing, and depth must be bounded and the bound REPORTED -- a resolver that silently truncates its own search reports a discharge it never established, which is ADR-007's line. EXTENDED RATHER THAN SPLIT. This bar carried a covers block declaring the per-bar judgement uncovered, and deliberately wired split_to into nothing so a new mechanism would not be used to close issues in the change that introduced it. That review has now happened and the judgement is made, so the bar is EXTENDED to cover it -- the second option completion.py's own resolution text names. Removing `covers` is only legitimate because the criteria below establish the work; removing it otherwise is what the resolution warns against. THE JUDGEMENT, per bar: 117 -> ['131'] and DISCHARGES, verified reading STOP_COMPLETE with BAR_COVERS_PART_DISCHARGED -- the first real use of the mechanism, on the bar whose own text records the by-hand split that motivated it. 155 -> ['156','165'] and 156 -> ['173','165'], neither discharging, which turns a prose dependency into a checked one. 93 and 143 get NO split_to and say why: their remainder was DEFERRED, not split. THAT DISTINCTION IS THE FINDING. `split_to` records where work WENT, never what it waits ON. Naming a blocker would make discharge mean 'the thing I waited for happened' rather than 'the work was done elsewhere', and would quietly turn every blocker into a discharge. My own plan for this work had 143 pointing at 150 and 146, which is exactly that mistake.

criteria.$comment: C11 EVERY COVERS BLOCK DECIDES ABOUT ITS OWN REMAINDER. Red at declaration: 154 and 171 declared uncovered scope with neither a split_to nor a stated reason for its absence. An absence with no reason is indistinguishable from an oversight, which is the state `covers` was built to replace.
criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] every covers block either splits or says why it does not"'

criteria.$comment: C12 A TYPO IS SILENT WITHOUT THIS. A malformed id names an authority that never completes, so the parent can never discharge and nothing says why.
criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] every split_to entry is a well-formed authority id"'

criteria.$comment: C13 THE WENT-TO VS BLOCKED-ON RULE IS WRITTEN DOWN WHERE covers IS DOCUMENTED. It cannot be checked mechanically -- it is semantic -- so the only defence is that a reader is told before they use the field.
criteria.target: bash -c 'grep -q "records where work WENT, never what it waits ON" references/dispositions.md'
bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] a covers block with no split_to still blocks completion"'
criteria.$comment: C1 NOTHING REGRESSES. Five of the six bars on disk have no split_to and must behave exactly as they did. This is the ADR-008 C7 shape applied to a decision path.

criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] split_to naming a complete authority discharges the covers block"'
criteria.$comment: C2 THE MECHANISM. Red at declaration -- split_to does not exist.

criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] split_to naming an incomplete authority does not discharge it"'
criteria.$comment: C3 THE CONTROL FOR C2. Without it, C2 passes by discharging everything, which turns `covers` into a comment and re-creates exactly what issue 133 was built to fix.

criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] an empty split_to does not discharge anything"'
criteria.$comment: C3b THE CHEAPEST WAY TO CHEAT. `split_to: []` is deleting `covers` with extra steps. all([]) is True, so this is the vacuous-truth trap that has appeared twice in this session already.

criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] a cycle is reported as a typed refusal, not a crash"'
criteria.$comment: C4 HAZARD ONE. 155 -> 156 -> 155 must not recurse. A stack overflow is not a governance disposition (ADR-005 rule 5).

criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] exceeding the depth bound refuses rather than truncating"'
criteria.$comment: C5 HAZARD TWO, and the more dangerous one. A resolver that silently stops searching and reports success declares a discharge it never established -- ADR-007's line exactly. Truncation must be a refusal, never a shrug.

criteria.target: bash -c 'python3 conformance/acceptance.py | grep -q "\[PASS\] the verdict names which child authority is outstanding"'
criteria.$comment: C6 A reader must be able to act. 'CONTINUE, because of covers' sends nobody anywhere; 'CONTINUE, because 156 is not complete' does.
C8 the completion firewall and the schema still hold; this touches the decision path.
